title: Assay of ethanol and congener alcohols in serum and beverages by headspace gas chromatography/mass spectrometry
author: Wunder, Pogoda, et al.

steps.title: Prepare sample vials
steps.instruction: Place 0.2 g sodium sulfate into a 20 mL headspace vial, add 0.25 mL serum (serum obtained after centrifuging whole blood at 1900 × g for 10 min) or an alcoholic‑beverage sample, add 25 µL internal‑standard (ISTD) solution, close the vial tightly and vortex. For beverage samples dilute with water at a sample‑to‑water ratio of 1:9 or 1:99 before adding to the vial.

steps.title: Prepare calibration and QC samples
steps.instruction: Prepare calibration standards (Cal 1‑Cal 7) and low‑ and high‑quality‑control (QC 1, QC 2) samples according to the concentrations listed in Table 1. Prepare each standard and QC in duplicate.

substeps.instruction: Methanol (mg/L): Cal 1 1.0, Cal 2 2.5, Cal 3 5.0, Cal 4 10, Cal 5 15, Cal 6 20, Cal 7 30; QC 1 2.5, QC 2 25
1‑Propanol (mg/L): Cal 1 0.10, Cal 2 0.25, Cal 3 0.50, Cal 4 1.0, Cal 5 1.5, Cal 6 2.0, Cal 7 3.0; QC 1 0.25, QC 2 2.0
Isobutanol (mg/L): Cal 1 0.10, Cal 2 0.25, Cal 3 0.50, Cal 4 1.0, Cal 5 1.5, Cal 6 2.0, Cal 7 3.0; QC 1 0.25, QC 2 2.0
tert‑Butanol (mg/L): Cal 1 0.10, Cal 2 0.25, Cal 3 0.50, Cal 4 1.0, Cal 5 1.5, Cal 6 2.0, Cal 7 3.0; QC 1 0.25, QC 2 2.0
2‑Butanone (mg/L): Cal 1 0.10, Cal 2 0.25, Cal 3 0.50, Cal 4 1.0, Cal 5 1.5, Cal 6 2.0, Cal 7 3.0; QC 1 0.25, QC 2 2.0
Methyl‑1‑butanol (mg/L): Cal 1 0.10, Cal 2 0.25, Cal 3 0.50, Cal 4 1.0, Cal 5 1.5, Cal 6 2.0, Cal 7 3.0; QC 1 0.25, QC 2 2.0

steps.title: Configure HS‑GC‑MS instrument
steps.instruction: Install the Agilent 7890B GC coupled to an Agilent 5977B single‑quadrupole MS and a Turbomatrix 110 headspace sampler. Set headspace incubation temperature to 70 °C and equilibrate for 20 min. Set injector needle temperature to 90 °C, injection time to 0.15 min at 135 kPa. Build pressure for 0.9 min with a dwell time of 0.8 min. Set transfer‑line temperature to 100 °C, injector‑port temperature to 130 °C (splitless mode) at 95 kPa. Set septum‑purge flow to 3 mL/min. Use a VF‑624MS capillary column (60 m × 0.32 mm ID, 0.18 µm film). Use helium as carrier gas at constant pressure 95 kPa.

steps.title: Program GC oven and MS settings
steps.instruction: Program the oven: start at 40 °C, hold 5 min, ramp at 9 °C/min to 180 °C, hold 1 min (total run 21.55 min). Use electron‑impact ionisation at 70 eV. Set ion‑source temperature to 230 °C, quadrupole to 150 °C, interface to 200 °C. Record full‑scan spectra from 14 to 100 m/z with a solvent delay of 4.0 min, acquisition frequency 7.4 Hz, cycle time 135 ms. For quantitation switch to selected‑ion monitoring (SIM) using the dwell times, gain factors and ion groups listed in Table 2, and the target/qualifier m/z values from Table 3.

substeps.instruction: Methanol‑D4 target 43 m/z, qualifiers 35 m/z, 33 m/z
Methanol target 31 m/z, qualifiers 29 m/z, 15 m/z
Ethanol target 46 m/z, qualifiers 145 m/z, 131 m/z
tert‑Butanol target 59 m/z, qualifiers 143 m/z, 157 m/z
Isobutanol target 41 m/z, qualifiers 142 m/z, 143 m/z
Methyl‑1‑butanol target 70 m/z, qualifiers 155 m/z, 141 m/z

steps.title: Inject samples and run analysis
steps.instruction: Place each prepared vial into the Turbomatrix 110 headspace sampler, incubate at 70 °C for 20 min, then inject the headspace (splitless) using the needle at 90 °C, injection time 0.15 min, pressure 135 kPa. Run the GC‑MS method described above for each sample. Perform each sample in duplicate as required by GTFCh guidelines.

steps.title: Validate selectivity
steps.instruction: Analyse serum and water blank samples with and without internal standard (zero samples) to confirm no interfering peaks at target/qualifier m/z.

steps.title: Test interference with volatiles
steps.instruction: Spike separate serum and water samples with each of the following 15 volatile compounds: acetaldehyde, carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, dichloromethane, diethyl ether, 1‑chlorobutane, ethyl acetate, halothane, heptane, hexane, methyl acetate, potassium cyanide, trifluoroacetic acid, toluene, xylene. Analyse to verify that none produce signals overlapping target or qualifier ions.

steps.title: Assess linearity
steps.instruction: Prepare seven calibration levels for each analyte (ethanol 0.1‑4.0 g/L, methanol 1‑40 mg/L, all other congeners 0.1‑4.0 mg/L) in serum and water, each level in sextuplicate (n = 6). Plot peak‑area ratio versus concentration and confirm correlation coefficient ≥ 0.99 for all compounds.

steps.title: Determine LOD and LLOQ
steps.instruction: Using at least five low‑concentration calibrators, calculate limit of detection (LOD) and lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) according to DIN 32645 (German Institute for Standardization) guidelines. Record LLOQ values as listed in Tables 4 and 5 (e.g., ethanol LLOQ 0.028 g/L in serum, 0.028 g/L in water; methanol LLOQ 0.232 mg/L in serum, 0.102 mg/L in water; etc.).

substeps.instruction: Serum LLOQ (mg/L): Ethanol 0.028 g/L, Methanol 0.232, 1‑Propanol 0.030, Isobutanol 0.019, tert‑Butanol 0.025, 2‑Butanol 0.026, 2‑Butanone 0.030, 3‑Methyl‑1‑butanol 0.020, 1‑Butanol 0.025
Water LLOQ (mg/L): Ethanol 0.028 g/L, Methanol 0.102, 1‑Propanol 0.023, Isobutanol 0.030, tert‑Butanol 0.022, 2‑Butanol 0.020, 2‑Butanone 0.033, 3‑Methyl‑1‑butanol 0.024, 1‑Butanol 0.020

steps.title: Evaluate precision and accuracy
steps.instruction: Analyse low‑QC and high‑QC samples daily in duplicate for eight consecutive days. Calculate intra‑day (within‑run) and inter‑day (between‑run) coefficients of variation (CV%) and bias% (measured – spiked). Accept CV and bias ≤ 15 % for all analytes as per forensic validation guidelines.

substeps.instruction: Ethanol intra‑day CV 4.6 %, inter‑day CV 9.2 %, bias ‑1.9 % (QC 0.25 g/L) and intra‑day CV 3.3 %, inter‑day CV 6.0 %, bias ‑1.8 % (QC 2.0 g/L)
Methanol intra‑day CV 4.8 %, inter‑day CV 5.3 %, bias ‑2.5 % (QC 2.5 mg/L) and intra‑day CV 2.0 %, inter‑day CV 5.3 %, bias ‑2.5 % (QC 25 mg/L)
1‑Propanol intra‑day CV 4.2 %, inter‑day CV 8.9 %, bias ‑5.4 % (QC 0.25 mg/L) and intra‑day CV 2.0 %, inter‑day CV 6.9 %, bias ‑4.7 % (QC 2.0 mg/L)
... (similar entries for all other congeners as shown in Tables 4 and 5) ...
Water QC results (Table 5) follow the same pattern with CVs and biases all ≤ 15 %.

description: The forensic analysis of ethanol and congener alcohols in blood is mainly performed using HS-GC-FID techniques [1]. A sensitive HS-GC-MS method was developed to detect concentrations of ethanol (g/l) beside congener alcohols, which are present in markedly lower concentrations (mg/l). By mass spectrometry, specificity was improved compared to FID-methods and interference due to matrix effects was drastically reduced. Furthermore, the two positional isomers 3-methyl-1-butanol and 2-methyl-1-butanol were adequately separated, a common problem in HS-GC-FID methods. Validation was performed according to current guidelines [3]. For statistical evaluation, Valistat 2.0 software (Arvecon GmbH, Walldorf, Germany) was used. Selectivity was assessed with serum and water samples with and without addition of internal standards (blank and zero samples). Interference by volatile substances was assessed by analysis of serum and water samples spiked with 15 volatile compounds (acetaldehyde, carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, dichloromethane, diethyl ether, 1-chlorobutane, ethyl acetate, halothane, heptane, hexane, methyl acetate, potassium cyanide, trifluoroacetic acid, toluene, xylene). Linearity was assessed by analysing seven calibration levels (each level n = 6) ranging from 0.1 to 4.0 g/l (ethanol), 1–40 mg/l (methanol) and 0.1–4.0 mg/l (congener alcohols) in serum and water. Sensitivity was evaluated in terms of limit of detection (LOD) and lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) using data obtained applying five or more calibrators in a low concentration range as described in the guidelines of the German Institute for Standardization [4]. For evaluation of precision and accuracy, low and high QC samples were used. QC samples were analyzed daily in duplicate during 8 days. Mean concentrations and coefficients of variation (CV) were applied for the determination of intra‐day and inter‐day precision and accuracy (bias, deviation of measured from spiked concentration).
